841.title: Curse the day (Job 3)
841.hook: Job curses the day he was born, and the Bible keeps every word
841.howItsDone: Jewish tradition has a long practice of lament: the book of Job, Lamentations read on Tisha b'Av, and psalms that question God are all part of the Tanakh and are read and studied aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three friends sat on the ground with Job for seven days and seven nights. Your line was they said nothing. When did you let a silence stay? Today, the silence breaks, and Job is the one who breaks it. Day eight hundred forty-one.

Seven days of quiet, and then: "After this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day." Two chapters ago, this same man said the LORD gave and the LORD hath taken away, blessed be the name of the LORD. The adversary bet he would curse. Now he opens his mouth, and the first thing that comes out is a curse. But read it closely, because the text is precise about the target. Not God. His day. The day he was born. Everything he's been holding since the messengers came is about to pour out.
screen: `AFTER THIS OPENED JOB HIS MOUTH.` → `HE CURSED HIS DAY.` → `NOT GOD. HIS DAY.`

segments.voice: Listen to how he starts: "Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived." He wants that day erased from the calendar. "Let that day be darkness; let not God regard it from above, neither let the light shine upon it." Then he goes further, and it's hard to hear: "Why died I not from the womb?" If only he'd never lived. Then he'd be lying still, he says, in the place where the small and the great are together, where the prisoners rest. "There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest." This isn't a man being polite to heaven. It's a cry, the whole chapter of it, and it ends with no answer and no resolution. Here's the thing to notice. This is scripture. The Tanakh didn't cut it, soften it, or add a note telling Job to calm down. His rage sits inside the holy books, read and studied, word for word. The Writings also hold Lamentations, and psalms that ask God how long. A tradition that keeps words like these is saying something about what may be said, out loud, in front of God. It doesn't mean Job is right about everything. The friends will argue with him, and so will God. But the book lets him say it first. If your own grief has ever come out angry, you're in the company of a man the book itself called perfect and upright.
screen: `LET THE DAY PERISH.` · `WHY DIED I NOT FROM THE WOMB?` · `THE WEARY BE AT REST.` · `SCRIPTURE KEEPS EVERY WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: allow one honest anger. Settle, and breathe. Is there something you're angry about that you've been keeping polite? A diagnosis, an injustice, a person, a year that went wrong. Let it come up. Say it to yourself in plain words, no softening. This isn't the time to act on it, or send the text, or decide it's wrong to feel. Just let it be said, inside, the way Job said his. Feel where it sits in your body. Breathe into that place. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is, rough edges and all. The bell holds the time.
Curse the day. After seven silent days, Job opens his mouth and curses the day he was born, and the book keeps every word. Today's word.
Your line: rage is allowed. Today, if anger comes, name it honestly to yourself before you decide what to do with it. Day eight hundred forty-one.

options: thank them for coming.
curse the day you were born.

fork.reveal: "let the day perish wherein I was born." not a curse on God, but on his own birthday, and the book keeps every word.

what it means: a man the book calls perfect and upright curses the day he was born, and scripture keeps his words.

842.title: Don't explain their pain (Job 4–5)
842.hook: the friends insist the innocent never suffer
842.tomorrow: I would speak to the Almighty
842.howItsDone: Jewish teaching on comforting mourners, drawn partly from Job's friends, warns against explaining a death or a loss to the bereaved; visitors are encouraged to listen and let the mourner lead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job broke seven days of silence by cursing the day he was born. Your line was rage is allowed. Did you name an anger honestly? Today, his friend answers him. Day eight hundred forty-two.

"Everything happens for a reason." It gets said at hospital bedsides and after funerals, by kind people who want to help. Eliphaz is that kind of person. He's the first of Job's friends to speak, and he starts gently, almost apologizing: "If we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved? but who can withhold himself from speaking?" In plain words: I know this might hurt, but I can't keep quiet. He reminds Job that he's comforted others, strengthened weak hands, steadied stumbling knees. And now it's come to you, he says, and you're shaken. Then he asks his real question.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAPPENS FOR A REASON.` → `ELIPHAZ SPEAKS FIRST.` → `WHO CAN KEEP FROM SPEAKING?`

segments.voice: Here it is: "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?" In other words, name one innocent person who was ever destroyed. You can't. So think about what that means for you, Job. Eliphaz backs it with what he's seen: "they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same." He even describes a vision in the night, a spirit gliding past his face, his hair standing up, a whisper asking whether any mortal can be more just than God. And by chapter five he's offering hope on the same terms: "Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth." Take the correction, and you'll be restored. Here's what makes this hard. Much of what Eliphaz says sounds like wisdom you could hear anywhere. Good things grow from good seeds. God is greater than we are. But he's saying it to a man sitting in ashes, scraping his skin, whose children are dead. And aimed at him, every general truth becomes an accusation: you must have done something. And we, the readers, know what Eliphaz doesn't. Chapter one told us: Job is perfect and upright, and his suffering began with a question asked in heaven, not with anything he did. Eliphaz has a theory that explains the world, and he needs Job's suffering to fit it. The book won't let it fit. Later, at the very end, God will say the friends haven't spoken rightly. For today, just notice how the explaining starts: kindly, reasonably, and from a friend who sat in silence for seven days.
screen: `WHO EVER PERISHED, BEING INNOCENT?` · `THEY THAT PLOW INIQUITY REAP IT.` · `A GENERAL TRUTH, AIMED AT ONE MAN.` · `WE KNOW WHAT ELIPHAZ DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: This one is harder than it sounds: don't explain someone's suffering to them. Settle, and breathe. Remember a time someone explained your pain to you. Maybe it was meant kindly: it was meant to be, at least you have, God doesn't give you more than you can handle. Notice how it landed. Now, more honestly, remember a time you did it to someone else. No need for shame. Just see it. Then think of one person who is hurting now, and try out what you might say instead. I'm here. I'm so sorry. Tell me. Let the explanations fall away, one breath at a time. If you pray, you can pray for that person without trying to make sense of it. The bell holds the time.
Don't explain their pain. Eliphaz tells Job that the innocent never perish, and turns a true-sounding rule into an accusation. Today's word.
Your line: don't explain their pain. Today, when someone tells you what hurts, skip the reason and the bright side, and just stay with them. Day eight hundred forty-two.

screen: `DAY 842 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: I WOULD SPEAK TO THE ALMIGHTY.`

843.title: I would speak to the Almighty (Job 13:3)
843.word: I would speak to the Almighty
843.hook: Job demands a hearing with God
843.carry: I would speak to the almighty
843.howItsDone: Jewish tradition includes prayer that questions and argues with God, from Abraham at Sodom and Moses after the golden calf to Job, and these texts are read and studied as part of the Tanakh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eliphaz asked who ever perished being innocent. Your line was don't explain their pain. Did you manage to just stay with someone? Today, Job has heard enough explaining. Day eight hundred forty-three.

By chapter thirteen, each of the friends has had a turn to explain, and Job has had it with them. "Ye are forgers of lies," he tells them, "ye are all physicians of no value." Doctors who can't heal. Then a line that's almost funny, if it weren't so tired: "O that ye would altogether hold your peace! and it should be your wisdom." If you'd just stay quiet, that would be your wisdom. It's hard not to hear the seven silent days behind it. And then he turns away from them entirely, because the friends aren't the ones he needs to talk to.
screen: `PHYSICIANS OF NO VALUE.` → `HOLD YOUR PEACE.` → `JOB TURNS AWAY FROM THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the turn: "Surely I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to reason with God." The friends have been talking about God. Job wants to talk to God. Not to be lectured, not to guess. A hearing, face to face. The language that follows sounds like a courtroom. "Behold now, I have ordered my cause; I know that I shall be justified." He has prepared his case. He'll stand before God and argue it. And in the middle of all that defiance comes a line people quote in very different moods: "Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him." Read both halves together. Trust, and argument, in one breath. Job doesn't stop believing God is there. That's exactly why he won't stop talking. You only demand a hearing from someone you think is listening. This is an old thread in the Tanakh. Abraham, hearing that Sodom will be destroyed, asks God, "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" Moses argues for his people after the golden calf. Jewish tradition has room for prayer that pushes back, that brings a complaint, that says this isn't fair and I'm saying so to your face. Job isn't asking his friends to let him off. He's asking God to show up. And that's a kind of faith too, the kind that won't go quiet.
screen: `NOT ABOUT GOD. TO GOD.` · `I HAVE ORDERED MY CAUSE.` · `THOUGH HE SLAY ME, YET WILL I TRUST.` · `ABRAHAM ARGUED TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: state your case plainly. Settle, and breathe. Is there something in your life that doesn't seem fair? Not someone else's case. Yours. Say it in one or two plain sentences, inside, the way you'd lay out facts to a judge. This happened. This is what it cost. This is what I don't understand. No polishing, no apologizing for asking. If you pray, you can say it to God, in your own words, as plainly as Job did. If you don't pray, just say it to the quiet, and hear yourself say it. The bell holds the time.
I would speak to the Almighty. Job turns from his friends and asks for a hearing with God, to argue his case face to face. Today's word.
screen: `I WOULD SPEAK TO THE ALMIGHTY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: I would speak to the almighty. Today, when something feels unfair, say it plainly to the one who can actually answer, instead of complaining to everyone else. Day eight hundred forty-three.

844.title: My redeemer liveth (Job 19:25)
844.hook: a flash of hope in the middle of despair
844.howItsDone: Jewish readers study Job 19:25 alongside the go'el, the redeeming kinsman of the Torah and the book of Ruth, and God is called redeemer, go'el, in the Tanakh and in daily Jewish prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job turned from his friends and asked for a hearing with God. Your line was I would speak to the almighty. What did you say plainly? Today, in the middle of that argument, a light comes on. Day eight hundred forty-four.

Chapter nineteen finds Job very low. His brothers are far from him, he says. His friends have forgotten him. His servants treat him like a stranger. His breath is strange to his own wife. Then he begs, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me." And then a wish. He wants his words to last. "Oh that my words were now written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book! That with an iron pen and lead they were graven in the rock for ever!" Carve it in stone, so somebody, someday, knows what happened to me.
screen: `FORGOTTEN BY FRIENDS.` → `HAVE PITY UPON ME.` → `CARVE MY WORDS IN THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: Then, with no warning, this: "But as for me, I know that my Redeemer liveth, and that He will witness at the last upon the dust." From the bottom of the pit, I know. The Hebrew word for redeemer is go'el. The same word runs through the book of Ruth, just days ago. Boaz was the go'el, the kinsman with the right and the duty to buy back a family's land and keep a dead man's name alive. In the Torah, a go'el is the relative who steps in when you can't help yourself and buys back what you lost. So Job, forgotten by his brothers and his friends, says: there is someone who will stand up for me. Who? The text doesn't say, and readers have heard it more than one way. Some hear God himself, the God Job is arguing with, somehow also the one who will defend him. Some connect it to a line a few chapters earlier, "my Witness is in heaven," and hear a defender on Job's side in the heavenly court. Christians read this verse too, and hear it about Jesus. The lines right after it are hard Hebrew, and translations of them differ. But the first half, I know that my Redeemer liveth, stands clear. And notice where it comes. Not after his health returns. Not after an answer. In the middle of being forgotten, Job says, I know. Hope here isn't the end of the pain. It's a flash inside it. And Job's wish came true in its own way: his words were written in a book, and people are still reading them.
screen: `MY REDEEMER LIVETH.` · `GO'EL: THE KINSMAN WHO BUYS BACK.` · `GOD, OR A WITNESS IN HEAVEN?` · `HOPE INSIDE THE PAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold on to one hope. Settle, and breathe. If something in your life feels heavy right now, let it be there. You don't have to push it away. Then, inside it, look for one hope. It doesn't have to be big. Someone who will stand up for you. A morning you're looking forward to. A belief that holds you. A person who remembers you. Find one, and hold it the way Job held his: not instead of the hard thing, but right in the middle of it. Breathe in, and hold it. Breathe out, and don't let go. If you pray, you can say Job's line, I know that my redeemer liveth. The bell holds the time.
My redeemer liveth. Forgotten by his friends, Job says there is a go'el, someone who will stand up for him, alive. Today's word.
Your line: my redeemer liveth. Today, write your one hope down somewhere you'll see it, the way Job wanted his words carved in the rock. Day eight hundred forty-four.

what a scholar hears: go'el, the same word as Boaz the kinsman in Ruth, the relative who buys back what you lost.

845.title: Where is wisdom? (Job 28)
845.hook: miners dig out gold, "But wisdom, where shall it be found?"
845.howItsDone: Job 28 is studied in Jewish tradition as a poem on wisdom, and its closing line, the fear of the Lord is wisdom, echoes a teaching found also in Psalms and Proverbs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, from the bottom of the pit, Job said I know that my redeemer liveth. Your line was my redeemer liveth. Where did you write your hope down? Today, the arguing stops for a while, and the book goes underground. Day eight hundred forty-five.

"Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold where they fine it." Chapter twenty-eight opens in a mine. Someone cuts a shaft far from where people live, and hangs on ropes, swinging, forgotten by anyone walking above. They turn the mountains over by the roots. They cut channels in the rock. They find sapphires in the stones and dust of gold. They go where no bird has gone: "There is a path which no fowl knoweth, and which the vulture's eye hath not seen." Down in the dark, they bring hidden things up into the light. Human beings, the poem says, can find almost anything.
screen: `A VEIN FOR THE SILVER.` → `HANGING ON ROPES IN THE DARK.` → `A PATH NO BIRD KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Almost. Then the turn: "But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?" We can dig to the roots of mountains, but nobody knows the way to that. The poem searches everywhere. "The depth saith, It is not in me: and the sea saith, It is not with me." Ask the deep. Ask the ocean. Not here. Can you buy it? The poem runs through the treasure room: gold, onyx, sapphire, coral, pearls, rubies, the topaz of Ethiopia. None of it is enough. Wisdom can't be bought, and it can't be dug up. Then where? "God understandeth the way thereof, and he knoweth the place thereof." Only God knows the way. And the chapter ends with what God says to human beings: "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding." Notice where this poem sits. Job and his friends have spent chapter after chapter arguing, the friends sure they know why Job suffers, Job sure they're wrong. Then this quiet poem drops into the middle, like a pause in a shouting match. Readers have debated who is speaking here: some hear Job, some hear the narrator stepping in. Either way it says something to everyone at the table: you can mine the earth, but you can't mine this. Wisdom here isn't a pile of answers. The friends had answers. It's a way of standing: in awe of God, and turned away from harm. It's what's left when the explanations run out.
screen: `WHERE SHALL WISDOM BE FOUND?` · `THE DEPTH SAITH, IT IS NOT IN ME.` · `NOT FOR GOLD OR RUBIES.` · `GOD UNDERSTANDETH THE WAY THEREOF.`

segments.voice: Put down the pickaxe for a minute, and look for understanding, not answers. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one question in your life that you've been trying to solve. Why did this happen. What should I have done. Notice how hard you've been digging. Now set down the shovel for a moment. Instead of asking for the answer, ask a different question: how do I want to stand while I don't know? Gently. Honestly. Turned away from harm. Let that be enough for this breath, and the next. If you pray, you can bring the question to God and leave it there for now. The bell holds the time.
Where is wisdom? People can dig gold out of the dark, but the poem in Job twenty-eight says only God knows the way to wisdom. Today's word.
Your line: where shall wisdom be found. Today, when you catch yourself digging for an answer, pause and ask how you want to stand instead. Day eight hundred forty-five.

what it means: humans can dig out gold, but wisdom can't be mined or bought; only God knows the way.

846.title: Out of the whirlwind (Job 38–39)
846.hook: God answers with stars, sea and wild goats: "Where wast thou?", and no explanation
846.howItsDone: Jews read God's speeches from the whirlwind near the end of the book of Job, and Jewish readers have understood them in more than one way, as rebuke, as comfort, and as an answer that is God's presence rather than an explanation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a poem went down into the mines and asked where wisdom could be found. Your line was where shall wisdom be found. When did you stop digging for an answer? Today, Job finally gets the hearing he asked for. Day eight hundred forty-six.

For chapter after chapter, Job has demanded it. Let God come. Let me lay out my case. And the friends have answered for God, again and again. Then, after all of it: "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind, and said." A storm. A voice out of the storm. The whole book has been waiting for this moment. Job has his speech ready. The reader has questions too: will God mention the adversary, the test, the children, the boils? Will God explain? And the first thing God does is ask a question back.
screen: `JOB DEMANDED A HEARING.` → `A VOICE OUT OF THE STORM.` → `WILL GOD EXPLAIN?`

segments.voice: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." And then the questions keep coming, wave after wave. Who measured the earth? Who stretched the line on it? Who laid its cornerstone, "When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?" Who shut in the sea with doors, and told it, "Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed"? Have you walked the springs of the sea? Have you seen the storehouses of the snow? Can you bind the Pleiades, or loosen the bands of Orion? Then God turns to the animals. The lioness hunting for her cubs. The raven's young crying out for food. "Knowest thou the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth?" The wild donkey that laughs at the city. The ostrich, the horse, the hawk. And this detail: God sends rain "on the wilderness, wherein there is no man." Rain where no human will ever see it. Here's what God never says. Nothing about the adversary. Nothing about the test. No reason for the boils or the house that fell. Job asked why, and God answered with the universe. Readers hear this in different ways. Some hear a rebuke: who are you to question me? Some hear a strange comfort: the world is far bigger than Job's pain, and God cares for corners of it no human has ever visited, wild goats giving birth on a cliff with no one watching. Both readings agree on one thing. Job asked for a hearing, and he got one. God came.
screen: `WHERE WAST THOU?` · `WHEN THE MORNING STARS SANG.` · `WILD GOATS, AND RAIN WHERE NO MAN IS.` · `NO EXPLANATION. GOD CAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at nature and let it be bigger than you. If you can, go to a window, or step outside. Find something you didn't make: the sky, a tree, a cloud, a bird, even a weed in a crack. If you can't move, picture the night sky. Settle, and breathe. Let the questions from the whirlwind come. Where was I when this was made? Do I know when the wild goats give birth? Who waters this? No need to reply. Just look. Let your own worries stand next to something much larger, and see how they sit there. If you pray, you can simply look, and let the looking be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Out of the whirlwind. God answers Job from a storm, with stars, sea and wild goats, and asks: where wast thou? Today's word.
Your line: where wast thou. Today, look up at the sky once, on purpose, and remember how much goes on that you'll never see. Day eight hundred forty-six.

847.title: Job spoke right (Job 42:7–17)
847.hook: God says the friends were wrong and Job was right; Job prays for them
847.howItsDone: Job belongs to the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh. Jews read and study it as a book that argues with God about suffering, and some readers take its last chapter as a model of praying for those who wronged you.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the voice out of the whirlwind asked Job about stars and sea and wild goats. Your line was where wast thou. Did anything outside make you feel small, in a good way? Today, the last chapter of Job, and the end of the week. Day eight hundred forty-seven.

Three friends sat with Job in the dust. For a long stretch of the book they argued with him. You must have done something, they said. God is just, so your suffering has a reason. Confess, and it will get better. Job refused. He cursed the day he was born, he demanded a hearing, he called out to God. Then God spoke from the whirlwind, and Job went quiet. A reader might expect the verdict to fall on Job. It falls somewhere else.
screen: `THREE FRIENDS WITH ANSWERS.` → `JOB REFUSES THEIR ANSWERS.` → `THE VERDICT FALLS ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: After the whirlwind, God turns, not to Job, but to Eliphaz, the first of the friends. In the words of the King James text: "My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." Read that slowly. The friends defended God. They said all the careful, tidy things. And God says they were wrong. Job accused, protested, wept, and asked why. And God calls him my servant, and says he spoke right. Readers still puzzle over this. What exactly did Job get right? Some say it was his honesty: he would not pretend his suffering made sense. Others say it was that he spoke to God, while his friends only spoke about God. The text doesn't settle it, and this path won't either. Then comes a second turn. The friends are told to bring an offering, and Job, the man they lectured, is to pray for them. And the text says something striking: the LORD turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends. His restoring begins there, in a prayer for the people who hurt him. The rest of the chapter is quick. His family and old acquaintances come to eat bread with him and comfort him. He is given twice as much as he had before. He has daughters again, and the text names them: Jemima, Keziah and Keren-happuch, and says their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers. Some readers find this happy ending too neat. Others hear it as a gift that never erases what was lost. Either way, the book ends with Job old and full of days. Job spoke right.

segments.voice: Before the bell, a look back at this week in Job. A cursed day. Friends explaining pain. A man asking to speak to the Almighty. A redeemer who lives. Wisdom that can't be bought. A whirlwind. Now today's practice. Bring to mind someone who hurt you, maybe with words that were meant to help. Not the worst person in your life; someone ordinary, who got it wrong while trying. Say their name once, inside. If you pray, you can pray for them, in your own words or with words from your tradition. If you don't, you can simply wish them one good thing today. The bell holds the time.
Job spoke right. God's verdict at the end of the book: the friends with neat answers were wrong, and the man who cried out was right. Today's word.
Your line: job spoke right. Today, when someone is hurting, resist the tidy explanation, and if someone has hurt you, try one kind thought toward them. Day eight hundred forty-seven.
